content:
Earlier this year, I swapped out a gas-powered push mower for a robotic lawn mower controlled by an iPhone. Users can manually drive the machine along the perimeter of the yard to build a virtual map. Once set up, the machine automatically handles mowing on a preset schedule.

Recently, I've been testing another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation approach, and after several weeks of testing, I believe this one may be the easier choice for many people.

Camera-driven automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year lies in how each machine understands your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I needed to manually drive the mower along the boundary with my iPhone to create the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses a system the manufacturer calls TerraVision 2.0. Three cameras allow the mower to automatically map the lawn, with no need for buried boundary wire or a separate RTK antenna.

The automatic approach to building the initial map takes longer. However, I feel that for people who aren't particularly tech-savvy, this method may be simpler.

To verify this claim, I had my mum in another state set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my help. She replied that everything worked well. But I'm not entirely sure she'd have the patience to first manually drive the robot around the entire boundary with her iPhone, then mark out each area to avoid.

Automatic mapping did introduce a small quirk in my front yard. There's no fence or other physical separation between my lawn and my neighbour's, so the TerraMow initially included part of the neighbour's lawn in my map.

I marked that section as a no-go zone in the app and that solved it. That said, if there's no clear visual boundary between lawns, you need to pay extra attention during the initial mapping.

A look through the mower's cameras

The cameras on the TerraMow also enable one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a live view of what the mower sees while it's working.

During testing, I used iPhone Mirroring on my Mac to keep this feed open in a large window. I could work indoors while watching from the mower's perspective as it moved around the backyard.

This feature isn't essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more fun, and occasionally helps explain why the mower slows down or avoids certain things. The Anthbot M9 doesn't offer a similar camera view.

The two iPhone apps share quite a lot in common otherwise. Both support scheduled jobs, mowing mode adjustments, zone划分, marking no-go areas, and remote-controlling the mower.

The TerraMow has one particularly nice variation on that last feature. In addition to the traditional left and right virtual joysticks, its app offers a single-handed joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone normally and use your thumb to guide the mower.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone isn't the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically on a preset schedule without any intervention. That said, the TerraMow's joystick mode is a lot of fun for clearing small patches it missed.

At times, I almost felt like I was controlling the robot with telekinesis (the fun kind, that is). Walking alongside the mower, iPhone at my side, thumb barely moving, and the machine was already following my direction.

All robotic mower apps should copy this control design.

A more aggressive mower

The TerraMow V1000 also feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was louder while working.

I wouldn't call the TerraMow "noisy," but the difference is noticeable. The Anthbot runs very quietly, to the point where it's easy to forget it's still going, including when it uses its headlight to mow after dark.

Because the TerraMow relies on camera navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. As a result, scheduling daytime mowing becomes more important.

The V1000 itself feels solidly built and is larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage that covers the charging dock, while Anthbot's garage is a separate purchase.

Most importantly, the TerraMow performed reliably. I relied on it for several straight weeks without having to step in and handle the routine mowing myself.

When adaptive mapping gets too clever

The same visual intelligence that makes the TerraMow easy to set up can occasionally backfire.

The mower constantly adjusts the map based on what it sees. After each job, saving these changes takes some time, during which you temporarily can't do anything else in the app.

After several consecutive days of rain, I ran into an interesting edge case. A section of the yard had pooled water, and the TerraMow understandably avoided that area during its next run.

The grass inside the skipped circular patch grew taller. Over time, the mower seemed to treat that growth as something to keep avoiding, ignoring the area even after the ground dried out.

I used the remote-control feature in the app to manually drive the mower and clear the taller grass, which fixed the problem. Once that patch returned to its normal appearance, automatic mowing resumed working there as usual.

Regular edging also helps the TerraMow reach the boundary with more confidence. Tall grass growing along an ambiguous line might otherwise be mistaken for an obstacle rather than part of the mowing area.

The Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more heavily on boundaries and obstacles defined by the user. This method requires more upfront work, but it also avoids the map "changing its mind" about a patch of grass.

9to5Mac take

After using both systems, for most people, I prefer the TerraMow's camera-based approach.

Burying boundary wire is completely out of the question for me, and installing an RTK base station means additional hardware to place, power, and maintain. The TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation isn't flawless. The initial map takes longer to create, a property line invisible to the naked eye needed manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook overgrown grass for a permanent obstacle.

These issues are still manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers simpler setup, reliable automatic mowing, a compelling live camera feed, and the best manual control I've used in a robotic mower app.

I do genuinely enjoy working in the yard, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing that off to a robot lets me spend my time on landscaping, edging, and detail work, while still keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 does this well enough that I can recommend it, especially for anyone who wants a robotic mower without burying wire, installing an RTK antenna, or walking the entire yard with a phone from start to finish.

Amazon currently has the TerraMow V1000 listed at US$999 after a US$200 coupon on the site. It's also available on the TerraMow official website.
